articles.title_orig: Latin American leaders get face time with China at APEC Summit 2026
articles.title_zh: Latin American leaders get face time with China at APEC Summit 2026
articles.content_orig:
The Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit kicked off today in Shenzhen, China, with Mexico, Peru, and Chile as the only members present from Latin America.
The summit brings together business and political leaders from across the Asia-Pacific region to discuss economic cooperation and development.
Presidents Claudia Sheinbaum, Keiko Fujimori, and Jose Antonio Kast all made the trip to China, with varying political and foreign policy agendas to advance. Their shared priority, however, revolves around one aim: to strengthen ties with Asia, especially China, without incurring the wrath of the United States.
All three countries face renewed tariff pressure from the U.S. while China remains a leading or major trade partner for each, so maintaining an effective balancing act will be key.
All three leaders still have singular goals at the summit, with each gaining vital one-on-one talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Claudia Sheinbaum has flown to China amidst gridlocked negotiations with the U.S. over renewal of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), with U.S. tariffs on autos, steel, and aluminum a core friction in the talks.
Amidst these commercial tensions, her administration is aiming to diversify Mexico’s industrial base and bring greater Chinese investment to the country.
Following her face-to-face with Xi, Sheinbaum said the two had discussed “a new era of cooperation for the development of Mexico-China relations.”
Mexico imposed tariffs of up to 50% on select Chinese products starting January 1 of this year, seen by some experts as an outcome of U.S. trade pressures on Mexico. The latest meeting may signal a lessening of commercial barriers, but likely not without input from the Trump Administration’s USMCA negotiators.
Mexico will also formally receive the APEC 2028 hosting baton during the Shenzhen summit.
Keiko Fujimori also met with Xi today prior to the APEC Summit, announcing Chinese support of US$22.5 million for resources to combat the damaging effects of the El Niño weather pattern in the country.
Peru’s economy is far more reliant on trade with China than with the U.S., with 37% of exports destined for Chinese shores (more than double the U.S. share) and state-owned Chinese firms controlling both Lima’s electricity distribution and the Chancay megaport.
Fujimori has ruled out strategic alignment with any single world power, instead pursuing a “strategically balanced” foreign policy agenda.
Following the APEC Summit, she will travel to Japan to discuss critical minerals with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, pitching Peru’s rare earths as a valuable alternative to Chinese-controlled supply chains.
Jose Antonio Kast traveled to China despite plunging popularity at home and an economy near crisis. He will be forced to walk a delicate foreign-policy tightrope between China, its largest trading partner, and the U.S., its leading foreign investor.
Kast’s meeting with Xi was celebrated as the 10th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Chile comprehensive strategic partnership and the 20th anniversary of the start of their bilateral free trade agreement.
Curiously, there was no mention of efforts to reinstate the Chile-China Express submarine fiber-optic cable project meant to connect Hong Kong with the Concón/Valparaíso region.
Then-president Gabriel Boric suspended the project after diplomatic pressure from the U.S., with the Kast government inheriting the impasse and affirming the project remains afoot, according to comments from China’s ambassador to Chile Niu Qingbao .
The U.S. imposed an additional 12.5% tariff on certain Chilean imports in July of this year, although the U.S.-Chile Free Trade Agreement provides substantial exemptions.
Differing Politics, Similar Strategy
Despite diverging political orientations, with Mexico veering left and both Peru and Chile moving to the right in recent elections, all three leaders share the same broad strategy: expanded Chinese trade and investment in their economies without provoking outrage and threats from the Trump Administration.
Their strategy is buttressed by talks with other potential Asian partners at the summit and beyond, with Fujimori heading to Japan and Kast scheduled for a stop in Vietnam .
With the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting unfolding over the next two days, further deals for Latin America’s Pacific heavyweights may yet be announced.
Featured image description: The APEC 2026 summit in Shenzen, China.
Featured image credit: @APEC via X.
Ignacio Gutierrez is a contributing reporter at Latin America Reports. He is an analyst with the IMF and a freelance journalist based in Washington, D.C. Ignacio holds a Master's degree in international studies from Johns Hopkins and has reported on economic issues for Latinometrics and others.

articles.title_orig: Dow plunges 1,000 points heading into Nvidia earnings: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow plunges 1,000 points heading into Nvidia earnings: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares slipped on Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the company prepares to report earnings after the bell.
Huang said he is open to returning as Nvidia's CEO and that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his behavior.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber . "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang continued.
Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, following reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. Outlets also reported that Huang also had an affair with a vice president at the company and an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
Lawmakers also announced Tuesday that Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO drew more than 190,000 signatures , including Elon Musk . But Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday.
The chip giant is also facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members, the company said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's China data center curb advances despite Amazon, Google, Meta lobbying
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's China data center curb advances despite Amazon, Google, Meta lobbying
articles.content_orig:
Fears that artificial intelligence could trigger an economy-wide surge in layoffs persist, even as a recent backlash against the technology and supporting infrastructure threatens to complicate its ongoing buildout.
Widespread job cuts have emerged as a central concern now AI has become increasingly integrated into the economy, given its ability to automate certain tasks and potentially entire roles. Some research has linked AI to an increase in layoff announcements, and several high-profile companies have cited the technology when announcing major job cuts in 2026.
Economists at Goldman Sachs say an “AI-driven layoff wave” has yet to materialize but could still be on the horizon. In their recently published 2027 U.S. outlook, cited by Fortune , the economists said they expect a “slightly softer low-hire, low-fire form of full employment” to persist through next year, before “AI displacement begins to have a larger impact in subsequent years.”
This comes as opposition to AI—in part fueled by employment fears—continues to gather momentum. Concerns about data centers , their electricity usage and water consumption have become a prominent political issue this year, with some viewing the backlash as a potential obstacle to the rapid expansion of AI and its impact on the labor market.
Data centers and the AI buildout became a central issue in some state and local races ahead of the 2026 midterms , serving as a proxy for broader affordability concerns. This created electoral difficulties for some candidates who had supported data-center expansion, while voters also backed measures restricting development. According to J.P. Morgan Asset Management, 40 of 41 local ballot measures involving data centers went against development.
In a post-election analysis , Nicol Turner Lee and Darrell M. West of the Brookings Institution wrote that the results “may lead to more policy shifts around data center development and the broader tech sector itself.”
Researchers have also explored how public opposition and regulatory restrictions could slow AI adoption and potentially limit its impact on employment.
In an analysis for the Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE), Era Dabla-Norris and Anton Korinek contrasted a “runaway scenario” involving widespread job displacement with one in which “regulatory friction” and “public skepticism” prevent ubiquitous AI adoption and keep labor market effects “manageable.”
Following the midterms, J.P. Morgan global market strategist Stephanie Aliaga wrote that “the AI buildout was on the ballot this year, and it lost.”
“Building out AI infrastructure was already a massive undertaking, with significant hurdles around power, permitting and financing,” she continued. “Growing political resistance adds to the difficulty, potentially bringing longer negotiations, higher costs and further delays.”
However, she added that pre-election efforts to slow the buildout had either been temporary or “struggled to advance.”
The latest monthly layoff figures from outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas show that AI has been widely cited as a reason for job cuts this year. Through October, the technology had been cited in 121,401 announced job cuts, around 20 percent of the year's total, making it the second-most cited reason behind economic conditions, which accounted for 130,531. The report also records 1,265 AI-cited cuts in October alone.
However, some experts are skeptical that AI will cause catastrophic disruption to the labor market .
“Right now, AI looms large as technology that can automate workflows and replace workers, but it often seems like it is being used as a convenient boogey-man that CEOs use to justify the cuts they want to make to increase shareholder value,” Kate Fortmueller, an associate professor at Georgia State University who researches labor in the film and television industries, told Newsweek in early November.
According to an October report from TIAA, AI is “adding a new layer of uncertainty to retirement readiness,” alongside rising costs and increasing longevity. Of those surveyed, 40 percent said they considered AI in the workplace a threat to their retirement plans, rising to 51 percent among Gen Z respondents .
Goldman Sachs economists have also pointed to previous recessions as a warning of how technological change can affect employment.
“History also suggests that the full consequences of AI for the labor market might not become apparent until a recession hits,” they said. “In past recessions, employment of workers in routine occupations has dropped sharply—especially when they followed productivity booms—and did not recover after.”
Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here .

articles.title_orig: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.title_zh: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook will not participate in an upcoming White House hearing to examine allegations she made false statements on mortgage documents unless concerns about the process are first addressed, her lawyer said in a letter to the White House obtained by CBS News.
Abbe Lowell, Cook's lawyer, told White House counsel Will Scharf that Cook has "no legal obligation" to appear at what he said is an "unfair" hearing before a three-member committee of Trump administration officials that is set for next month. He warned participating in the proceeding would undermine the Fed's "unique status" and independence.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," Lowell wrote.
His letter to Scharf revealed that the two sides have exchanged numerous communications in the weeks since President Trump announced that he had created a "committee of inquiry" to look into the claims that Cook made misrepresentations on mortgage forms related to two properties before joining the Fed's Board of Governors in 2022.
The committee is made up of Kevin Hassett, assistant to the president for economic policy; Andrea Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, director of the Office of Government Ethics.
Cook has repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said Mr. Trump is attempting to remove her from the Fed because he disagrees with her decisions on interest rates.
"It is unfortunate that your latest correspondence fails to address the concerns Governor Cook has previously raised — making clear that you are uninterested in convening the 'substantive and fair hearing' you have claimed. Instead, you seek only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome," Lowell wrote.
Cook had raised concerns in earlier letters to the White House about Hassett's membership on the committee because of comments he has made about the Fed governor, which Lowell said "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
"Mr. Hassett's continued presence on the Committee remains unacceptable," Lowell said.
He also took issue with the White House's proposed process to exchange documents. Lowell said it is "fundamentally unfair" because it would require Cook to hand over documents immediately, while she would not gain access to information that the White House has until seven days before the hearing.
Lowell had also pressed the White House on the specific legal standard the committee would apply to determine what constitutes "cause" to remove a Fed governor and the participation of Justice Department personnel in the hearing, he said.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
Mr. Trump first tried to fire Cook in August 2025 after Bill Pulte, the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, accused her of making false statements on mortgage applications. Cook filed a lawsuit claiming that her removal was in violation of federal law, which allows the president to remove a member of the Fed's board only "for cause."
The Supreme Court in June allowed Cook to remain in her job while her case continued and found that Mr. Trump failed to provide Cook with the procedural protections she was entitled to under the law, namely notice of the allegations against her and the opportunity to respond before she was fired.
Weeks after the Supreme Court's 5-4 decision, Mr. Trump again moved to oust Cook. The White House said in a letter to Cook in August that the president was considering terminating her because of the mortgage fraud accusations and gave her a chance to respond — seemingly an attempt to remedy the issues raised by the Supreme Court.
The president then announced last month that he had established the committee to look into the claims against Cook and determine whether he has cause to remove her.
The hearing at the White House was initially set to take place Nov. 5, with committee members set to consider evidence and allegations against Cook.
In his latest letter to Scharf, Lowell said the White House had attempted to schedule a hearing on dates that conflicted with the Fed's official business. He said that Scharf claimed in an Oct. 19 letter that if Cook didn't show up on the date selected by the White House, the hearing would proceed without her and the committee could "draw an adverse inference" from her failure to appear because of official obligations.
"To be clear, if the White House establishes an unbiased panel and implements fair procedures that do not prejudge the outcome — such as providing the evidence it claims to have gathered with sufficient time for review and response — Governor Cook would be prepared to appear," Lowell wrote. "But the ultimatums in your November 2, 2026 letter do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation."

articles.title_orig: Trump kicks off Asia trip with first stop in the Philippines
articles.title_zh: Trump kicks off Asia trip with first stop in the Philippines
articles.content_orig:

President Donald Trumparrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila , the Philippine capital, is Trump’s first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin , and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un .
Trump administration details its $50 billion request for aviation system improvements
The Trump administration has formally updated its request to lawmakers for $50.1 billion to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system and to make other improvements at airports.
A letter to key lawmakers dated Tuesday says that less than 24 hours after the administration’s request of $30.1 billion, “the urgent need for this investment became undeniable.” That’s when outdated equipment disrupted aircraft communications and radar feeds, forcing the Federal Aviation Administration to initiate a nationwide ground stop.
The request to lawmakers calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation’s air traffic control system. Another $10 billion would go to boosting airport infrastructure.
Meanwhile, $10 billion would go to replace or refurbish terminals at high-impact hubs. Another $10 billion would go to construct five new traffic control centers and $10 billion would go to improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.
Trump’s pick to lead the Navy focuses on shipbuilding in his opening statements
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told senators at his confirmation hearing Tuesday that he’ll focus on revitalizing shipbuilding in an effort to expand the nation’s fleet of warships.
But Cao avoided potentially thorny topics that are likely to come up before the Senate Armed Services Committee. Those include the Iran war, the recent firings of Navy admirals and the waiver Cao will need from Congress to become Navy secretary because he left active duty less than seven years ago.
Cao also spoke of his biography, which includes fleeing Vietnam with his family right before the fall of Saigon in the 1970s. He also focused on his 25 years of service in the Navy.
“I spent my entire adult life serving in the United States Navy special operations community with multiple combat deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan and Somalia,” Cao said.
Bipartisan concerns arise over forces being ‘stretched thin’ during Navy secretary hearing
Despite deep divisions over the Iran war, the Republican and Democratic leaders of the Senate Armed Services Committee voiced a unified concern over the impact the ongoing military operation and internal issues at the Department of Defense have had on the U.S. Navy.
“Our sailors and Marines are our greatest asset, but they cannot sustain an increasingly demanding operational tempo without adequate support,” GOP Sen. Roger Wicker, the committee chair, said during his opening statement.
His Democratic counterpart, Sen. Jack Reed, echoed his worry, saying that “disruption” from high-ranking officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, “sends the wrong signal to our sailors and Marines.”
Confirmation hearing for Trump’s nominee to lead the US Navy gets underway
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, appeared Tuesday before the Senate Armed Services Committee as he seeks the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. It’s the first step in a nomination process that could turn into a fierce debate over the Iran war, military transparency and the well-being of American sailors.
Cao also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago.
ASEAN-US dinner menu features American surf and turf
The main course was a pairing of U.S. beef tenderloin and lobster tail, served with a truffle potato puree, glazed baby carrots, oyster mushrooms and a wine sauce, according to details shared by the White House.
Courses before the main included ratatouille, goose liver mousse and burrata cheese salad with heirloom tomatoes, walnuts, balsamic glaze and olive oil.
Chocolate-covered cake with roasted almonds and salted caramel ice cream was served for dessert.
Trump’s pick for Navy secretary likely to face Iran war questions during confirmation hearing
He’s scheduled to testify before a Senate committee Tuesday, the first step in a nomination process that could turn into a fierce debate over the Iran war, military transparency and the well-being of American sailors.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, is seeking the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. He also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago.
Cao will face the current Congress, with Republicans still in charge. But he’s likely to face intense scrutiny from Democrats over aspects of the Iran war, including major damage to the service’s 5th Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, as well as the recent firings of Navy officials.
Trump could meet Imelda Marcos during summit in Philippines
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion between Trump and an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she’s well enough and gets her doctors’ nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet-set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 “People Power” public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: “How’s Imelda?” Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
“Personal connections are very important to him,” Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. “President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, ‘Please say hello to your mother,’” according to Romualdez.
US and Thailand sign joint statement affirming terms of forthcoming trade deal
At a brief signing ceremony in Manila, Trump said Thailand has agreed to eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports and remove “substantial” nontariff barriers on American automobiles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry.
Trump said Thailand will also be buying an estimated $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products and “that makes our farmers very happy.”
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said there’s still “a little more to do” before the agreement itself is finalized and that it should be “ready for us to sign real soon.”
Trump still talking about possible meetings with Russia, North Korea leaders
Trump says North Korea’s leader would like to meet with him in China later this week. And he’s open to sitting down with Russian President Vladimir Putin, too.
But so far, it appears neither meeting has been arranged.
Trump landed in the Philippines on Tuesday for talks with Asia-Pacific leaders. On Thursday, he’s due in Shenzhen, China, for more talks, including a historic three-way confab with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“We’ll see what happens,” Trump said in Manila when reporters asked about North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

articles.title_zh: Take-Two lays off Firaxis employees on eve of Grand Theft Auto VI launch
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
As gamers anxiously await this week’s release of Grand Theft Auto VI , Fox News hosts are already starting the culture wars over the crime-fueled video game series.
Fox & Friends Weekend hosts Rachel Campos-Duffy, Charles Hurt and Griff Jenkins recently looked at a preview of the new game , featuring characters Jason Duval, an Army veteran working for local drug runners, and Lucia Caminos, who was previously jailed after fighting for her family.
“I’m gonna push back a little,” Campos-Duffy, wife of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy , said. “I’m not thinking that this is a good thing for our culture.”
Jenkins then suggested Campos-Duffy could play as Luicia, prompting her to ask, “Is she the hooker?”
“No, she’s a partner-in-crime,” Jenkins said. Campos-Duffy then laughed it off. “You can maybe play and get her to go straight,” Jenkins added.
Conservatives and liberals have long fought over cultural beliefs, typically when it comes to civil rights, including diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and LGBTQ+ issues.
Fox News is known to promote the conservative view, railing against DEI and trans rights. And now, the network is coming after your favorite video game.
In Grand Theft Auto VI , set to be released at midnight on Thursday, Jason and Lucia will find themselves in the middle of a criminal conspiracy in the fictional state of Leonida, where they will need to rely on each other to make it out alive.
Grand Theft Auto , or GTA for short, is one of the most popular gaming franchises of the century. GTA fans have been waiting more than a decade for a new game in the series, making Thursday’s release even more exciting for them.
Roughly 15 million copies of Ground Theft Auto VI have been preordered, CNN Business reported, citing Sensor Tower data.
Strauss Zelnick, the CEO of GTA’s publisher, Take-Two Interactive, told Variety that presales of the new game are “running far in excess of our expectations.”
Violent games like GTA , Call of Duty and Mortal Kombat have faced scrutiny over the years for potentially leading to bad behavior in players, such as aggression.
But a study published in Molecular Psychiatry in 2018 found no changes in behavior between participants who played Grand Theft Auto V , the non-violent video game The Sims 3 and those who played no game at all.

articles.title_orig: Apple, Google and more services down in latest wave of widespread outages
articles.title_zh: Apple, Google and more services down in latest wave of widespread outages
articles.content_orig:
Apple said it was experiencing tech issues Tuesday that were affecting several of its popular consumer-facing services.
As of 2 p.m. ET, Apple’s own system status page showed that Apple Business, Apple School Manager, AppleCare, iCloud Mail and Web Apps, and SchoolWork were each experiencing outages.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
Earlier, the page showed the App Store and Apple Music experiencied outages.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” an Apple spokesperson told NBC News. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
At Apple stores in New York and Chicago, employees told NBC News earlier in the day that their internal software had stopped working and they had been unable to complete purchases or make appointments.
Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, was also having technology issues that guests reported had impacted reservations and check-ins, among other problems, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.
Marriott, which has 10,200 properties and more than 1.8 million rooms under its corporate umbrella, did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Associated Press.
Gmail also appeared to experience an outage briefly Tuesday, with some users reporting issues accessing their email, according to Downdetector. The issue did not appear to be widespread and the company posted on X that they weren't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption."
The outages come on the heels of a string of major disruptions impacting U.S. services over the past several days — including Monday's Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo banking disruptions and United Airlines departing-flight system glitch , following Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop and Thursday's Microsoft cloud outage.
President Donald Trump brushed off the recent outages that wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails, saying Tuesday, “it’s life.”
“It’s life, it’s life,” he told reporters during his trip to the Philippines when asked about the outages. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”
While none of the issues appear to be related, they’ve exposed America’s reliance on older infrastructure and revealed the extent to which companies and governments are being forced to upgrade systems in the AI age. The incidents have also stoked unfounded paranoia that something larger may be afoot.

articles.title_orig: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.title_zh: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.content_orig:
The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.
The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years. Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have also surged.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".
Criticising the move on X, he wrote that Israel - as it has done in the past - will respond with "countermeasures", and that "decisions will be announced in due course".
"Israel will not bow to external pressure or change its policies as a result," Saar said, adding that they will "consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities" in the West Bank, and "protect those involved in developing and building".
Israel previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".
The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and called on other countries to follow suit.
It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.
Responding to the announcement, the group said: "Tzav 9 is a movement of abiding citizens from all the political spectrum, and we've always protested peacefully."
It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.
The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.
"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.
"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."
In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
At the time, Miliband said the move marked the beginning of a "new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".
That announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel , which said it would shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation.
Last month, most diplomats left the consulate - which handled UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza - but the UK insisted that the building would not be closing and would operate as a "UK mission".
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.title_zh: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain
articles.content_orig:
The official said the strikes are in response to IRGC attacks.
Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.
Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
The U.S. conducted airstrikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Tuesday, targeting launchers in response to IRGC targeting of U.S. personnel and assets, according to a U.S. military official.
"U.S. Central Command remains highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region," the official said.
A tanker transiting in the Strait of Hormuz was reportedly struck for a second time, which caused a fire onboard, a maritime security agency reported to the UKMTO.
This comes after a third party reported an attack on the same vessel on Monday, which resulted in the vessel being disabled and resulted in an engine room fire, according to the UKMTO.
The crew are currently unaccounted for and a damage assessment is currently unknown, according to the UKMTO.
"Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO, whilst authorities investigate," the UKMTO said in an update Tuesday.
U.S. Central Command said on Tuesday that air defenses defeated an Iranian drone attack that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said targeted an American radar facility in Bahrain.
"Multiple Iranian one-way attack drones launched by the IRGC today towards Bahrain were intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel. CENTCOM and partner forces remain highly vigilant," the command said in a post to X.
The Bahrain Defence Force said on Tuesday morning that it "intercepted and destroyed" several Iranian munitions launched at the Gulf kingdom.
The BDF statement came shortly after Bahrain's Interior Ministry issued a safety alert for residents. The attack is the third Iranian strike on Bahrain in the past week.
In a statement published by the semi-official Fars News Agency, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it attacked the Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain using drones, targeting an American radar system there.

articles.title_orig: Waymo barred from operating on California freeways following viral I-280 incident
articles.title_zh: Waymo barred from operating on California freeways following viral I-280 incident
articles.content_orig:
The California Department of Motor Vehicles has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard.
The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them.
One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times.
The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after images showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month.
VIDEO: Driverless Waymo tries to bypass CHP traffic break on SF freeway
In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority.
"Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told ABC7 Eyewitness News.
The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026 , Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones.
The California DMV says these new restrictions went into effect on November 11 and "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions..."
"I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco.
Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop.
MORE: Study finds lower crash rate for Waymo vehicles in San Francisco
"An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said.
Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. ABC7 Eyewitness News previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again Monday.
"I used to use it all the time and now it's like ehh I'll walk, or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said.
Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue.
"You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.

articles.title_orig: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.title_zh: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.content_orig:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.
“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the company said .
The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
Critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own New Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.
However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The issue may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.
ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.
The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the investigation, which is being led by ULA. Again, this information is preliminary, and no definitive conclusions can or should be drawn.
This was the fifth flight of the Vulcan rocket since its debut in January 2024. Two of the previous flights have experienced issues with the nozzles on its solid rocket boosters, but in both cases, the rocket was able to compensate for the reduced and asymmetric thrust and reach its intended orbit. The second nozzle issue caused Vulcan to stand down for nine months.
This latest setback is likely to sideline Vulcan for at least half a year, and probably longer. Most impacted will be the US Space Force, which has national security payloads waiting for a ride to space on Vulcan, and Amazon, which had more than a dozen launches of its Amazon Leo constellation on the manifest for 2027. It would exacerbate a worsening launch crisis in the United States.
There are potentially serious implications for Blue Origin as well, which is seeking to return New Glenn to flight as early as January. Last Tuesday, the company said a modified BE-4 main oxygen valve had successfully completed qualification testing.
“Our modified valve has already been incorporated into engines slated for upcoming flights, and we are now rolling it out across the remaining fleet,” the company said . “We expect to complete the anomaly investigation later this month.”
If Vulcan’s failure were ultimately due to a problem with the BE-4 engine, it would certainly delay the New Glenn rocket’s return to flight. This would be a setback not just for Blue Origin but for NASA, which is counting on the super heavy lift rocket to do much of the heavy lifting for its Artemis Program and Moon Base.

articles.title_orig: The first pill to slow Alzheimer’s could come from an unexpected place
articles.title_zh: The first pill to slow Alzheimer’s could come from an unexpected place
articles.content_orig:
AriBio’s erectile dysfunction med-turned Alzheimer’s disease candidate mirodenafil has delivered some mixed results from a global phase 3 trial.
In patients with early Alzheimer’s disease, AriBio’s mirodenafil candidate, AR1001, delivered better clinical outcomes than placebo did—but only in a subgroup of patients who were not on any background therapies such as an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor or memantine, according to results from the Polaris-AD trial.
In the overall population, including those receiving other therapies at baseline, the trial missed statistical significance on change in the Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) at week 52. The data were shared at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer Disease conference in Boston.
The trial is technically positive, as it’s designed with dual primary populations, each with its separate statistical significance bar. AriBio said it plans to discuss the results with the FDA.
Digging into the readout, among 604 patients in the prespecified monotherapy population, AR1001 performed 0.44 points better versus placebo, with a p-value of 0.0266 meeting the prespecified statistical significance threshold of 0.03. This translated into a 31% slowing of clinical decline, according to AriBio. For the entire trial of 1,535 patients, the treatment difference came in at 0.11 points lower on CDR-SB in favor of AR1001, or a 7% slowing of decline, but the p-value reached 0.4015, failing the prespecified statistical significance bar of 0.02.
“We started developing AR1001 with the goal of creating an oral treatment that could slow Alzheimer’s progression and be practical for patients and care partners to use over the long term,” Jai-Jun Choung, Ph.D., chairman and CEO of AriBio, said in a Nov. 16 statement. “The 31% slowing of clinical decline at one year in the Monotherapy population supports our hypothesis.”
AR1001 showed numerical advantage on secondary cognitive and functional measures in the monotherapy population, including a treatment effect of 1.16 points versus placebo on the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale 13 and a 0.7-point difference on the Mini-Mental State Examination.
With the phase 3 readout, the ball is now in Fosun Pharma’s court. The Chinese pharma paid South Korea’s AriBio $60 million in May for an option to potentially in-license AR1001, a PDE5 inhibitor like Viagra, in the U.S., Europe and Japan. Fosun has 90 days after receiving full Polaris-AD data to decide whether to exercise its option, which will trigger up to $180 million in upfront and regulatory milestone payments.
Originally developed by SK Chemicals Life Science, mirodenafil has been approved in Korea since 2007 for erectile dysfunction. AR1001 uses a lower dose of the drug at 30 mg taken daily. The drug works differently than antibodies such as Eisai and Biogen’s Leqembi and Eli Lilly’s Kisunla, which directly target amyloid-beta plaques in the brain.
By inhibiting PDE5, mirodenafil prevents the breakdown of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), which promotes neuron survival and synaptic plasticity. As a brain-penetrant small molecule, the drug can also dilate cerebral blood vessels, potentially improving blood supply to the brain, while theoretically helping the brain clear toxic protein aggregates like amyloid-beta.
Supporting those mechanisms, the Polaris-AD trial showed that AR1001 increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cGMP levels versus placebo after one year in both the overall and monotherapy populations. CSF p-tau217 results numerically favored AR1001, but no difference in the CSF Aβ42/40 ratio, which evaluates the presence of amyloid plaque, was observed.
It’s difficult to compare AR1001’s data with anti-amyloid antibodies because of different trial designs. Previously, in the phase 3 Clarity AD trial, Leqembi achieved a 0.45-point difference versus placebo on the CDR-SB metric at 18 months, slowing clinical decline by 27%. About 60% of patients in that study were taking symptomatic Alzheimer’s medications at baseline.
Both Clarity AD and Polaris-AD targeted patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease, although the baseline characteristics of cognitive impairment were different.
In an interview with Fierce in June, Fosun Pharma’s CEO of the firm's innovative medicines division, Xingli Wang, M.D., Ph.D., highlighted low dropouts from the Polaris-AD trial, as well as a high rollover rate into the trial's extension period, as positive signs.
In a Nov. 16 release, AriBio described AR1001 as “generally well tolerated.” Over the one-year double-blind treatment phase, serious adverse events happened in 10% of patients in the AR1001 arm, versus 9.8% in the control arm. Deaths happened in four (0.5%) of patients receiving AR1001 and two (0.3%) receiving placebo. Adverse events led to discontinuation of study drug in 5.2% of AR1001-treated participants and 1.7% of placebo-treated participants.
“Polaris-AD has given us important phase 3 data, including results in the prespecified monotherapy population, as well as safety data, for a once-daily oral therapy that could offer patients a convenient treatment option,” Wang said in a Nov. 16 statement. “We will remain patient-centered and, based on the complete body of evidence, continue to work closely with AriBio on the full dataset.”
“The CDR-SB finding in the prespecified monotherapy population and the safety profile are encouraging. The secondary endpoints and biomarker findings warrant further evaluation alongside the overall population outcome to understand AR1001’s therapeutic effects in early Alzheimer’s disease,” Sharon Sha, M.D., of Stanford University and principal investigator of Polaris-AD, said in a statement. “The work of Polaris-AD is another step towards filling an unmet need in early Alzheimer’s disease in which patients need more options for treatment.”

articles.title_zh: Apple confirms iCloud outage as users report issues with Apple Pay, App Store and other services
articles.content_orig:
Apple appears to be experiencing issues with its online services today, preventing some users from signing into iCloud and other Apple services. According to Downdetector , a site that tracks reports of online service outages, iCloud, Apple Support, Apple Pay, and the App Store are all seeing spikes in reports. Apple's support page currently shows it's having issues with iCloud accounts and sign-ins, along with other services.
According to Downdetector reports, these are the services that saw spikes in outage reports:
"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," an Apple spokesperson told us in a statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible."
In addition to iCloud, Apple's support page also flags that AppleCare on Device, which lets you purchase AppleCare on your phone or tablet, is experiencing an outage. That's alongside Apple Business, Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps and Schoolwork
As of 1:10 p.m. ET, the page also listed the App Store and Apple Music as experiencing an outage. Around 1:41 p.m. ET, the affected services on Downdetector started showing a downward trend in reports, indicating they may be recovering.
Users online reported being signed out of services and unable to sign back in. Others reported being unable to activate new iPhones.
The issues follow a string of outages that have plagued online services over the past week. On Nov. 12, Microsoft Outlook and Teams were knocked out for more than 30 hours due to what Microsoft described as a technical issue. On Nov. 13, a technical issue caused all air traffic across the U.S. to be grounded , leading to thousands of canceled and delayed flights.
On Monday, online services at several major U.S. banks experienced problems for several hours after an issue with JPMorgan Chase's systems. Today, CNN reported that a highly classified communications network used by the National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

articles.title_orig: Europe fears what Trump, Xi and Putin might discuss behind closed doors in China
articles.title_zh: Europe fears what Trump, Xi and Putin might discuss behind closed doors in China
articles.content_orig:
Three strongman leaders over age 70, 90% of the world’s nuclear weapons, two ongoing wars, one room, and no specific agenda. What could possibly go wrong?
What Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will discuss during their unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday is far from concrete. But that is perhaps the point. A high-level summit like this would usually establish clear outcomes ahead of time, and be the culmination of months of intense planning and signalling.
But whatever preceded the Shenzhen meeting matters little with the inclusion of a wild card like Trump. Nuclear non-proliferation was flagged as a main focus, though little progress is expected – to say nothing of “safeguarding world peace,” another agenda item according to China. Then suddenly, Trump mentioned Iran, Ukraine, Nvidia, and even floated a meeting with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
It’s not abnormal for world leaders to go off script. Yet it has rarely been as risky as it will be Thursday. Especially when it comes to Ukraine.
Trump referred to Europe’s longest ongoing war Monday with both a slip of a tongue and sarcasm. He called Ukraine “my favorite subject” and added, “Ukraine’s losing – Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month” – almost edging Russia’s horrific losses out of his sentence. Ukraine is for Trump the irritant that got itself invaded, hasn’t accepted his hurried and compromising peace, and is always losing.
The Shenzhen meeting is a risky moment not because Kyiv and its European allies will suddenly buckle under whatever declarations emerge; they have grown sufficiently inured to Washington’s fickle nature. The danger is in Trump’s desire to be liked by powerful authoritarians, what is agreed to in private, and how that informs Putin’s confidence and Xi’s perception of Trump’s mental health.
Putin has, for free, got his moment on the world stage, allowing him to present Russia, for a day, as the global superpower it once was, rather than the one it is brutally struggling to become again.
Anxiety among European officials is palpable. “Trump listens to the last person he talks to, so that will be a driver for what he says,” said one European official speaking to CNN on the condition of anonymity. A European diplomat said it was: “Hard to see anything good on European security to come out of this meeting.”
Another senior European official said the optics of the trilateral were “of course awful for us,” but was less concerned a wider deal would be struck.
The first official called the meeting a “Putin dream,” ushering in his rehabilitation on the world stage, and added a key issue for Trump would be “who stands in the middle of the big boys takeaway picture.”
That picture of the three leaders after their meeting will speak a thousand words about Western decline. The man who invaded Ukraine unprovoked nearly five years ago, his bankroller in chief, and the US president who has reversed decades of US policy to pressure Kyiv to accept a bad deal, through limiting military aid.
A key risk is Trump agreeing with a Russian narrative, or fictional presentation of the frontline facts, and feeling obliged to adhere to a deal he has hurriedly made with the two strongmen he not-so-secretly admires.
Many of the European officials CNN spoke to harbor distant hopes that Beijing may emerge as a good-faith arbiter in the war. It is a view born of Xi’s apparent pressure on Putin to curtail nuclear saber-rattling , China’s stopping short of the full-scale arming of Russia during the war, and Beijing’s ambition to become the global superpower that can enforce effective change.
But this rosy view overlooks how urgently China needs Moscow to not lose this war, to prevent another key ally from suffering humiliation, and how the US has ridden roughshod over Iran and Venezuela this year – two Chinese allies whose degradation Beijing might like to see avenged by the collective West suffering a defeat in Ukraine.
The past month has delivered repeated blows to Ukraine and European NATO countries, dressed in the guise of the US peace process, led by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and friend Steve Witkoff, two envoys who have limited diplomatic experience and even less diplomatic successes to their names. First, Trump struck a deal to buy Russian diesel, wiping away years of sanctions and opening the door to the replenishing of the Kremlin’s war chest. Then followed the mysterious stoppages in US intelligence sharing and Starshield services – vital to the nightly defense of Ukraine from Russian missiles – that the White House appears to have suggested either didn’t happen or shouldn’t have.
In a Kremlin meeting last month, Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian” after he released retired American teacher and US military veteran Stephen Hubbard.
Then Kushner, after meeting Putin’s envoy in DC, recast the peace process as a bid for a new European security infrastructure, pandering to the Kremlin narrative that the real belligerent is NATO next door - and not Russia, who invaded one neighbour, Georgia in 2008, and another, Ukraine, twice in 2014 and 2022.
After further Starshield restrictions were placed on Ukraine during a peace summit, Kushner flew to Moscow hoping Putin would “give his blessing” to Europe joining the trilateral peace talks. He emerged saying Putin had done so, only to be flatly contradicted by the Kremlin. And finally, Kushner appears to have suggested NATO-type security guarantees if Ukraine gives up the rest of the Donbas region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
And, this is just the stuff that is publicly known. It is not too far-fetched to see the Shenzhen summit as the pinnacle of Trump’s settling into Moscow’s orbit. His actions in public show no other course. He even suggested Putin could have been “a lot tougher” on Ukraine, a statement that can only nod to Russia’s nuclear arsenal, given its nightly exhausting of its conventional armaments into Ukraine’s skies.
This will not be a feared Yalta 2.0, in which global powers carve up the world. The first Yalta summit in 1945 divided the world after the worst conflict in its history, between three victors whose empires either crumbled or bloomed afterwards.
Different men will attend Shenzhen. Trump and Putin are fighting different and failing wars of choice, and are the aging embodiment of their nations’ waning power. Xi has overseen a brutal, staggeringly efficient and swift rise of a global tech superpower, but still flinches away from conflict in his own potential war of choice – the invasion of Taiwan.
History had no choice but to listen to Truman, Stalin and Churchill after World War II. It might choose to tune out Shenzhen.
But the damage need not come in the form of Trump parroting Kremlin talking points when he emerges. Or Putin being given a space on the world stage for his false historical lectures on Russian victimhood and supremacy. Or Xi – probably the largest-scale authoritarian in history – appearing to be the reasonable, calm one.
The gift to Moscow is in how little opposition Putin will feel. The two most powerful men in the world are likely to give him an easy ride in private, and not demand an immediate ceasefire or durable peace in Ukraine. Pressure will instead be focused on Ukrainian and European concessions. The peace process may suffer yet another curiously pro-Russian reset that buys the Kremlin months more to try and seize tiny pockets of the Donbas, or let Ukrainian mothers and children suffer through another freezing winter.
There is little time left for these aging leaders – Xi is 73, Putin is 74 and Trump is 80 – to change the world. Perhaps this is just a blip in the autocratic curve of history. But the ticking clock makes the remaining two years of this US presidency particularly perilous.

Just two weeks after Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colorado) lost reelection for his battleground House seat, heâs making plans to run again in 2028.
This time, it will be in a new district.
Evans, a first-term lawmaker who lost in a swing area north of Denver, said on social media Monday that he plans to seek the GOP nomination for an adjacent, redder seat where Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colorado) narrowly lost reelection .
The move could make Evans the second Colorado Republican to seek electoral refuge in the 4th District, which covers most of the stateâs rural Eastern Plains to reach the Denver area.
Boebert moved into the area, which voted for President Donald Trump by 18 percentage points in 2024, this election cycle to preserve her chances of staying in Congress as her first seat grew more competitive. She lost this month by less than one percentage point to Eileen Laubacher, a Democrat and retired U.S. Navy rear admiral.
Evans fell short by about 15 points to former state lawmaker Manny Rutinel in the perennially swingy 8th District, which has bounced between parties in recent years and which Trump won in 2024.
Evans did not say why he was not making another bid for his current seat, and a spokesperson for his campaign declined to answer questions on the topic. But in a statement, Evans stressed his family and business ties to the 4th District, where he grew up and graduated high school, and said his expensive race in the Denver media market already gives him high name recognition.
At least nine other House GOP candidates who lost this month, including six who were running for reelection, have filed paperwork to run in 2028.
President Donald Trump on Tuesday nominated Gen. Chris LaNeve to serve as the Armyâs top officer, setting the stage for a possible confirmation battle before Democrats take control of Congress in January.
LaNeve has served as the Armyâs acting chief of staff since April, after an unexpected ascent to the Pentagonâs top ranks in Trumpâs second term. LaNeve replaced Gen. Randy George, who was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in April without cause.
The Army, with nearly 1 million people in uniform and about 200,000 civilian employees, has gone without a confirmed chief of staff for five months amid doubts that LaNeve would have enough support in the Republican-led Senate to be confirmed to the job. U.S. officials said in August that Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), an Army veteran, was opposed to confirming LaNeve . George is a friend of hers and also from Iowa.
In August, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell downplayed the delay in nominating LaNeve, saying that administration officials were âactively coordinating with our Senate partners to lock in the optimal moment to formally submit his nomination, and we intend to do so.â
LaNeve was a three-star general serving in South Korea when Trump took office, and got the presidentâs attention by calling to congratulate him on his election when Trumpâs second term began in January 2025, officials have said. LaNeve was soon selected to serve as Hegsethâs top military assistant at the Pentagon, and then elevated again to the Armyâs No. 2 role in February 2026.
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT â One month after cancer surgery, Pope Leo XIVâs sense of humor appears to be as intact as his health.
The pope, who looked surprisingly strong on his grueling 12-day trip to South America, took the high road after a worshiper hit him in the eye with a thrown rosary at his final Mass in Lima, joking on his way back to Rome that it was a sign of the personâs âfaith.â
âThe dearness of the Peruvians, including the person with a lot of faith who simply wanted to offer me a rosary, may be the things that you carry in your heart â or maybe the eye â that mark the life of someone,â he said to chuckles from journalists.
âHere you have enthusiasm, here you have deep faith, you have a desire to receive the Blessing of the Lord,â he continued.
It is not uncommon for worshipers to toss items at the pope â rosaries, stuffed animals, handmade papal dolls â a practice viewed by some as endearing and by others as an accident waiting to happen. Days before being struck, Leo dazzled an audience in the capital by dexterously catching a rosary flung at him, then hurling it back to the thrower with the finesse of a point guard.
An estimated 81.5 million Americans are expected to travel for Thanksgiving next week, according to AAA.
The projected number of people traveling at least 50 miles from home between next Tuesday and the following Monday  represents a slight drop from last yearâs record-breaking figure of 81.6 million domestic travelers, the group said Monday , but would still surpass the previous high of 80.2 million in 2024.
The AAA predicts that the overwhelming majority of trips â 72.9 million â will be made by car, although it anticipates a drop of 200,000 from last year, in part because of high gas prices . Almost 6 million people are expected to fly.
âAfter three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year,â AAA Travelâs Vice President Stacey Barber said in a statement. âBut travelers wonât notice much of a difference ...  since projected volumes remain near record levels.â
The AAA created its forecast before Fridayâs nationwide ground stop led to the cancellation of thousands of flights.
However AAA spokesperson Aixa Diaz told the Associated Press that ground stop was unlikely to have a major impact on Thanksgiving travel, adding: âIt takes a lot to keep holiday travelers home.â
President Donald Trumpâs nominee to run the Navy faced sharp bipartisan questioning during a Senate confirmation hearing on Tuesday, as lawmakers accused the Trump administration of a lack of transparency and detailed long-term strains on the service.
Acting Navy secretary Hung Cao, who has been nominated to take the job on a permanent basis, appeared before the Senate Armed Services Committee and acknowledged that the months-long Iran war has posed significant challenges for the Navy fleet.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) said Cao was âfailing these sailors and their familiesâ following an outcry over the living conditions aboard ships involved in the conflict.
Cao responded that he does not control the length of deployments and looks at âeverything through one lens and one lens only: How will this affect my son, a United States Marine, all his fellow Marines and his shipmates.â
He later defended against criticism that ships were running out of food while deploying, saying no vessel has âever gotten to zero.â
âItâs like my kids opening up the refrigerator door and saying, âThereâs nothing to eat in here,â â Cao said.
Cao also was pressed by Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) about the administrationâs withholding of information from Democrats on the committee. Democrats, Rounds said, âwerenât invitedâ to some classified briefings and discussions, making it less likely that they would support a future supplemental defense spending bill.
âPretty tough to ask all of my colleagues to support that if theyâre not even invited in to hear the information in the first place,â Rounds said.
Cao agreed to being âopen and honest with the entire Senate and the Congress, also.â

articles.title_zh: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.
